title: China's Military Says AI Can't Replace Commanders. Xi Is Testing That
gist: Using a text-analysis corpus of over 145,000 PLA Daily articles, Jaehwan Lim shows China's Central Military Commission has been reduced from seven members to two (Xi Jinping and a career discipline officer) after successive purges removed every experienced military commander, even as the PLA's own newspaper insists with rising frequency that human commanders — not AI — must retain final battlefield authority; Lim argues the purges and the AI push are two sides of the same problem (Xi's distrust of his own officer corps), and that the PLA's press has a specific, telling blind spot: it discusses data-quality problems extensively but never connects purge-driven fear of honest reporting to the corruption of the data that would feed military AI.

insights.claim: On Jan. 24, 2026, China's Ministry of National Defense announced that Zhang Youxia (vice chairman of the Central Military Commission) and Liu Zhenli (chief of the Joint Staff Department) were under investigation for serious violations of discipline and law — they were the last two members of the seven-person commission with substantial operational experience.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: A dated, named purge event (Jan. 24, 2026) that removed China's last operationally experienced top military leaders — a hard catalyst for assessing PLA command competence and China's near-term willingness/readiness to initiate a major conflict (e.g., over Taiwan).

insights.claim: Of the six Central Military Commission members Xi Jinping appointed in 2022, five are now gone; only two remain — Xi himself, described as a military amateur, and Zhang Shengmin, a career discipline-inspection officer who has never commanded troops in the field.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the purge (5 of 6 appointees gone) and highlights that China's top military decision-making body is now effectively run by a non-military leader and a discipline officer — a structural readiness/competence risk factor for any near-term China military contingency.

insights.claim: The chief of the Joint Staff Department's chair — the nerve center of Chinese operational planning — has been left vacant for the first time since the Cultural Revolution.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: An extraordinary historical marker (first vacancy since the Cultural Revolution) signaling the depth of the PLA's current command crisis — a strong, rare signal worth weighing heavily in any near-term China-conflict-risk assessment.

insights.claim: With only two members left, the Central Military Commission cannot function as a party committee; analysts have likened the situation to firing all but one member of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, an arrangement under which no modern military could realistically operate.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: A vivid comparative benchmark (equivalent to gutting the U.S. Joint Chiefs to one member) for gauging just how dysfunctional China's top military decision-making apparatus currently is.

insights.claim: The hollowing-out extends beyond the commission: after Miao Hua was removed from his party and military posts in October 2025, the Political Work Department was left under a deputy director; only the Eastern and Central Theater Commands are now led by full generals, with lieutenant generals occupying posts that normally carry higher rank elsewhere; by one estimate, barely one-fifth of the military's key leadership positions are permanently filled while nearly half are occupied on an interim basis.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Quantifies the depth of PLA leadership instability across theater commands, not just the top commission (only ~20% of key posts permanently filled, ~50% interim) — a broad readiness-degradation signal relevant to assessing PLA operational reliability over the next several years.
insights.locator: The hollowing out extends well beyond the commission itself

insights.claim: Xi could reverse the vacancies quickly via a single Central Committee plenary session, a routine procedural step historically used for such reshuffles, but has chosen not to — implying he either accepts the readiness cost as worth political reliability, or increasingly views the commission as ceremonial now that the Chairman Responsibility System channels operational authority directly through him and his personal staff.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Frames the prolonged CMC vacancy as a deliberate, sustained choice by Xi rather than a temporary crisis — implying investors and analysts should not expect a quick institutional fix, and that Xi is centralizing operational command around himself.
insights.locator: Xi could reverse this quickly if he chose

themes.theme: What the PLA's own press says about AI and command

insights.claim: Lim's text analysis of a themed subset of roughly 57,000 PLA Daily articles (drawn from a corpus of over 145,000 published January 2018-June 2026) found that articles explicitly asserting the human commander's final authority over AI-enabled operations rose from 45 in 2018 to 153 in 2025 — a 3.4-fold increase.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: A rigorously quantified (3.4x) rising institutional insistence on human command authority even as AI adoption accelerates — a data point directly relevant to gauging whether China's AI-enabled command systems are actually trusted internally or remain aspirational.

insights.claim: Over the same period, AI-related coverage in PLA Daily expanded from 967 articles in 2018 to 2,513 in 2025, while the subset specifically linking AI to command roughly tripled — meaning growing enthusiasm for AI has not crowded out, but has been matched by, growing insistence on human final authority.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Shows the PLA's stance is not a fading holdover position but an actively reinforced doctrine growing in parallel with AI enthusiasm — relevant to assessing how far China's military is actually willing to delegate lethal decision-making to autonomous systems.

insights.claim: Within the PLA Daily corpus, arguments defending human command authority are framed in operational rather than political language by a ratio of well over 20 to 1 — invoking the commander, the battlefield, and the chain of command far more often than party leadership or political control.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Indicates the PLA publicly defends human command as a professional-responsibility issue (accountability for war) rather than explicitly as party-control doctrine — useful for interpreting future PLA Daily statements about AI and autonomy.
insights.locator: Procurement documents reveal what the Chinese military is buying

insights.claim: Foreign Affairs reporting (Bresnick, Probasco, and McFaul, March 2026) drawing on thousands of Chinese military procurement requests found China's political and military leadership does not fully trust the PLA's chain of command and may look to AI decision-support systems to compensate for what they describe as a 'weak and inexperienced' officer corps — a substitution thesis that receives almost no support within the PLA Daily corpus itself.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: A direct tension between external procurement-based analysis (AI substituting for a weakened officer corps) and internal PLA discourse (which rejects substitution) — implies China's AI-for-command-authority strategy is being imposed on the institution rather than organically endorsed, a risk factor for how effectively it will actually work.
insights.locator: Can AI Rescue a Military with a 'Weak and Inexperienced' Officer Corps?

insights.claim: PLA Daily discusses AI training-data problems intensively: 340 articles link AI to training data, data quality, sampling, or data governance, rising from 9 in 2018 to 77 in 2025, with 71 more in just the first half of 2026 — including warnings that skewed training data can cause a model to misallocate fire to secondary targets, or produce a 'high score, low ability' trap in evaluation.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Confirms the PLA is technically sophisticated about AI data-quality risk in the abstract — meaning any failure to connect this to purge-driven misreporting (see below) is a deliberate or institutional blind spot, not ignorance of AI data risk generally.
insights.locator: The Machines Will Eat What the Army Feeds Them

insights.claim: The Chinese term for data fabrication (数据造假) appears six times in all of 2025 but 24 times in just the first six months of 2026, while terms for false and concealed reporting run at 50 to 70 articles a year in the PLA Daily corpus — showing rising institutional alarm about fabricated data and reporting.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: A sharp, quantified 4x jump in data-fabrication terminology in early 2026 alone signals an accelerating internal PLA concern about falsified data — a leading indicator worth tracking for further evidence of readiness-reporting integrity problems inside China's military.
insights.locator: The Machines Will Eat What the Army Feeds Them

insights.claim: Across roughly 57,000 AI- and command-related PLA Daily articles, the paper never connects the political incentive to misreport created by purge campaigns to the corruption of the training data on which military AI depends — a link Lim searched for under multiple keyword formulations and found absent in every case, with all data-integrity discussions confined to civilian statistical fraud, adversarial manipulation, or technical dataset flaws.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, structural, and self-reinforcing failure mode in China's AI-enabled military modernization: purge-driven fear suppresses honest reporting, that corrupted data feeds AI decision-support systems, and the institution cannot even discuss the problem in its own press — a durable reason to discount the near-term reliability of China's AI-compensation strategy for its weakened officer corps.

insights.claim: This data-corruption vulnerability is not uniform across all Chinese military AI applications: it is concentrated in systems that ingest human reporting (readiness assessments, logistics data, personnel records), while systems trained largely on sensor data (targeting, computer vision, undersea tracking) are far less exposed, since an inflated readiness report is not among their principal inputs.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Gives a specific framework for differentiating which categories of Chinese military AI (human-reporting-dependent decision-support tools) are most likely to underperform due to corrupted data, versus which (sensor-fed targeting/tracking systems) remain more reliable — useful for calibrating threat assessments of specific PLA AI capabilities.
insights.locator: This problem is not general to all AI applications

insights.claim: New Central Military Commission disciplinary regulations issued at the end of 2025 explicitly warned against 'false war-preparedness' and 'fabricated training results,' alongside incomplete implementation of the Chairman Responsibility System — confirming the leadership knows units under pressure perform readiness rather than build it, yet neither the regulations nor the newspaper connect this to what it means for AI systems trained on that same data.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Provides direct regulatory confirmation (from China's own 2025 disciplinary rules) that fabricated readiness/training reporting is a known, named problem at the top of the PLA — strengthening the case that any China military AI system trained on internal reporting data carries a documented, leadership-acknowledged corruption risk.
insights.locator: The regime itself supplies the evidence

themes.theme: Interpreting the purges: competing views and the core thesis

insights.claim: Lim synthesizes and extends three existing analyses of the PLA purges published in War on the Rocks: Joel Wuthnow argues the disruption is temporary and the greater danger comes in the late 2020s when better-credentialed commanders arrive with less standing to push back against Xi's war optimism; Rob Pierce argues the purges are structurally inevitable and will produce scripted exercises and inflated readiness reporting; Christopher Nye argues destroying the military's informal networks produces atomization, leaving Xi to decide in an information environment divorced from reality.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Summarizes three distinct expert forecasts for how China's purge-driven command dysfunction will evolve — useful competing scenarios for war-gaming China's near/mid-term military reliability and Xi's decision-making environment.
insights.locator: What these vacancies mean has already been debated

insights.claim: Some analysts suggest Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were removed after clashing with Xi over the pace of military modernization, arguing genuine joint-operational capability cannot be built on political timelines — though the reason for their removal remains uncertain, one fact is clear: the capability gap they represented has not been filled.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Raises the possibility that Xi is purging officers specifically for resisting unrealistic modernization timelines — implying continued pressure toward accelerated, possibly premature, military readiness targets that outside observers should treat skeptically.
insights.locator: Why Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were removed remains uncertain

insights.claim: Lim's central thesis is that the purges and China's accelerating AI adoption are two expressions of a single problem — how Xi preserves control over a military whose operational competence he does not fully trust — with the purges reflecting distrust of human commanders and the AI push reflecting hope that machines can compensate for what the purges removed; he frames this as Xi's wager that technology can offset institutional damage from his own system of political control.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: The article's core investable framework: China's AI-military modernization push should be read as a hedge against self-inflicted command dysfunction rather than a pure capability leap, implying its effectiveness is capped by the same political dynamics undermining the human command structure it aims to compensate for — a reason for caution in over-weighting China's AI-enabled military capability in near-term threat models.
insights.locator: The purges and China's turn toward AI are therefore not separate developments

insights.claim: Lim argues the hollowing-out of the Central Military Commission is not simply a crisis Xi has failed to resolve, but one he appears willing to tolerate, given his capacity to reverse it quickly through routine party procedure and his choice not to do so.
insights.speaker: Jaehwan Lim
insights.so_what: Pushes back against a 'crisis Xi can't control' narrative in favor of a 'crisis Xi is choosing to sustain' narrative — a meaningfully different read for anyone forecasting whether/when China's top military leadership dysfunction will resolve.
